title: Bipolar Transistor Characteristics & DC Operating Point Analysis

content.aim: To determine the bipolar junction transistor's DC operating point (Q-point), investigate its fundamental terminal current-voltage characteristics in common-emitter configuration, and develop a comprehensive understanding of its physical behavior across different conduction regions (cutoff, active, and saturation) for linear amplification and solid-state switching applications.
objectives: Study the internal semiconductor physics, junction structure, charge-carrier transport mechanisms, and terminal conventions of an NPN bipolar junction transistor (2N2222).
Experimentally measure and plot the Input Characteristics (base current I_B versus base-emitter voltage V_{BE} at constant collector-emitter voltage V_{CE}).
Experimentally measure and plot the family of Output Characteristics (collector current I_C versus collector-emitter voltage V_{CE} for various constant base currents I_B).
Identify and delineate the boundaries of the three distinct operating regions: Cutoff Region, Active (Linear) Region, and Saturation Region.
Construct the DC Load Line on the output characteristic family using Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) and locate the quiescent operating point (Q-point).
Investigate the thermal stabilization role of the emitter resistor R_E by evaluating operating point shift when V_S is disconnected and when R_E is short-circuited.

theory.text:
Physical Structure & Charge-Transport Mechanisms of the BJT

The Bipolar Junction Transistor (BJT) is a three-terminal, current-controlled semiconductor device consisting of two back-to-back p-n junctions formed within a single crystal lattice. In an NPN transistor, a moderately thin, lightly doped p-type silicon layer (Base) is sandwiched between two heavily doped n-type silicon regions (Emitter and Collector). The operation depends simultaneously on two charge carriers of opposite polarities—electrons and holes—which gives the device its "bipolar" designation.

The three physical regions are engineered with distinct geometric and metallurgical doping profiles to optimize current amplification:

Emitter (E): Heavily doped (n^+) region. Its primary physical function is to inject a high concentration of majority carriers (electrons in NPN) across the forward-biased Base-Emitter junction into the base region.
Base (B): Extremely narrow physically (typically 0.5 to 1.5\,\mu\text{m}) and very lightly doped (p). The light doping ensures low majority hole concentration, minimizing electron-hole recombination within the base. The narrow physical width ensures that over 98\% to 99.5\% of the injected electrons transit rapidly across the base via thermal diffusion without recombining.
Collector (C): Moderately doped (n) region with the largest physical volume and cross-sectional area. Its function is to collect the injected minority carriers swept across the reverse-biased Base-Collector junction depletion region. Because the collector junction dissipates significant electrical power (P_D = V_{CE} \cdot I_C), the larger surface area facilitates effective heat dissipation to prevent thermal runaway.
Fundamental Current Equations & Amplification Factors

Applying Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) to the transistor terminals yields the exact governing relationship:

Terminal Current Relationship:

I_E = I_B + I_C
where I_E is the emitter current, I_B is the external base current supplying recombinations and reverse-saturation losses, and I_C is the total collector current. The collector current consists of two distinct components: the injected carrier current reaching the collector, and the minority leakage current (I_{CBO}) of the reverse-biased collector-base junction:

Collector Current Formulation:

I_C = \alpha \, I_E + I_{CBO}

\alpha = \frac{I_C - I_{CBO}}{I_E} \approx \frac{I_C}{I_E}, \qquad (0.95 \le \alpha \le 0.998)
In the common-emitter configuration, the transistor operates as a current amplifier where the small base current I_B directly modulates the much larger collector current I_C. Substituting I_E = I_B + I_C into the collector equation yields:

Common-Emitter Current Gain (\beta or h_{FE}):

I_C = \frac{\alpha}{1 - \alpha}\, I_B + \frac{I_{CBO}}{1 - \alpha} = \beta \, I_B + I_{CEO}

\beta = h_{FE} = \frac{\alpha}{1 - \alpha} = \frac{I_C}{I_B}
For modern silicon planar transistors such as the 2N2222, the reverse leakage current I_{CEO} = (\beta + 1)\, I_{CBO} is on the order of a few nanoamperes at room temperature (25^\circ\text{C}) and is negligible compared to the milliampere-range operating currents. Consequently, in the active linear region:

Linear Active Current Relation:

I_C = \beta \, I_B \qquad (\text{typically } 50 \le \beta \le 300)

DC Load Line Analysis & Quiescent Point (Q-Point)
When the transistor is placed into an external circuit with supply voltage V_{CC}, collector load resistor R_C, and emitter stabilization resistor R_E, the output loop is governed by Kirchhoff's Voltage Law:

Output KVL Loop Equation:


V_{CC} = I_C \, R_C + V_{CE} + I_E \, R_E
Since I_E = I_C + I_B \approx I_C (because I_B \ll I_C), the KVL equation simplifies to:

DC Load Line Equation:


V_{CC} = V_{CE} + I_C (R_C + R_E)

I_C = -\left(\frac{1}{R_C + R_E}\right) V_{CE} + \frac{V_{CC}}{R_C + R_E}
This represents a straight line plotted directly on the family of I_C versus V_{CE} output curves. Its geometry is defined by two fundamental boundary intercepts:

Cutoff Intercept (I_C = 0): At zero collector current, no voltage drops across R_C and R_E. Thus:


V_{CE(\text{cutoff})} = V_{CC} = +12.0\,\text{V}
Saturation Intercept (V_{CE} = 0): The theoretical maximum collector current occurs when the transistor acts as an ideal short circuit:


I_{C(\text{sat})} = \frac{V_{CC}}{R_C + R_E} = \frac{12\,\text{V}}{1000\,\Omega + 100\,\Omega} = \frac{12}{1100} = 10.91\,\text{mA}
The Quiescent Operating Point (Q-point) is the intersection of this DC load line with the specific characteristic curve corresponding to the DC base current I_B established by the base biasing network. For faithful, distortion-free linear amplification, the Q-point should reside near the center of the active region on the load line, allowing symmetric positive and negative signal swings without prematurely clipping into saturation or cutoff.

procedure: Initial Setup & Power Connection: Interconnect the TPS-3371 trainer module to the regulated DC power supply. Verify that the master switch is OFF.
Transistor Mounting: Insert the 2N2222 into the breadboard socket. Verify correct pin orientation (E, B, C).
Circuit Implementation (Circuit 1): Wire the DC biasing circuit:
Connect R_{B1} = 91\,\text{k}\Omega between +12\,\text{V} rail and Base.
Connect R_{B2} = 15\,\text{k}\Omega between Base and Ground.
Connect R_C = 1.0\,\text{k}\Omega between +12\,\text{V} rail and Collector.
Connect R_E = 100\,\Omega between Emitter and Ground.
Connect variable source V_S to the input node.
Energize & Calibrate: Adjust main rail to +12.00\,\text{V}.
Variable Input Voltage Sweep: Vary V_S from 0.1\,\text{V} to 1.2\,\text{V} in 0.1\,\text{V} steps. Record V_B, V_C, V_E.
Output Curve Plotting: Plot I_C vs V_{CE}. Delineate cutoff, active, and saturation zones.
Evaluation with V_S Disconnected (Circuit 2): Disconnect V_S. Measure quiescent V_B, V_C, V_E. Calculate I_C. Mark Q-point.
Evaluation with R_E Shorted (Circuit 3): Short R_E. Re-measure. Compute I_C = \frac{V_{CC} - V_C}{R_C}. Plot modified Q-point.
precautions: Device Pinout: Confirm TO-18/TO-92 pin configuration before applying power.

Power Dissipation Limit: Ensure V_{CE} \times I_C never exceeds P_{D(\text{max})} = 500\,\text{mW} at 25^\circ\text{C}. In our setup: P_D \approx 6.0\,\text{V} \times 5.25\,\text{mA} = 31.5\,\text{mW}, well within SOA.
De-energize during Rewiring: Always turn off supply before modifying connections.
DMM Impedance: Set voltmeters to \ge 10\,\text{M}\Omega input impedance to avoid loading the 91\,\text{k}\Omega / 15\,\text{k}\Omega divider.
Thermal Settling: Allow several seconds between adjustments for junction temperature stabilization.
content.discussion:
The experimental measurements for the 2N2222 NPN BJT provide rigorous confirmation of semiconductor transport theory in the common-emitter configuration.

In the Input Characteristics (I_B vs V_{BE}), the base-emitter junction behaves identically to an ideal forward-biased p-n diode. Below V_{BE} \approx 0.50\,\text{V}, the built-in potential barrier prevents majority electron diffusion, resulting in near-zero collector current (< 0.05\,\text{mA}). Beyond the knee voltage (V_\gamma \approx 0.65\,\text{V}), base current rises exponentially and the transistor enters the active region.

In the Output Characteristics (I_C vs V_{CE}), three distinct zones are visible:

Cutoff: I_B = 0, I_C \approx 0, V_{CE} \approx V_{CC} = 12.0\,\text{V}.
Active (Linear): Spans V_{CE} \approx 1.0\,\text{V} to 12.0\,\text{V}. Slight positive slope due to the Early Effect (base-width modulation), where increasing V_{CE} widens the CB depletion region, narrowing effective base width W_B.
Saturation: V_{CE} below \approx 0.3\,\text{V}. Both junctions forward-biased. Collector current limited by external components:

I_{C(\text{sat})} \approx \frac{V_{CC} - V_{CE(\text{sat})}}{R_C + R_E} \approx \frac{12.0 - 0.15}{1100} = 10.77\,\text{mA}
Analysis of Bias Modification & Role of R_E
Thevenin Base Equivalent (Circuit 2):

V_{TH} = V_{CC} \left(\frac{R_{B2}}{R_{B1} + R_{B2}}\right) = 12 \times \left(\frac{15\,\text{k}\Omega}{91\,\text{k}\Omega + 15\,\text{k}\Omega}\right) = 12 \times 0.1415 = 1.70\,\text{V}

R_{TH} = R_{B1} \parallel R_{B2} = \frac{91 \times 15}{91 + 15} = 12.88\,\text{k}\Omega
Quiescent Collector Current:

V_{TH} = I_B R_{TH} + V_{BE} + I_E R_E \approx I_B R_{TH} + V_{BE} + I_C R_E

I_C = \frac{V_{TH} - V_{BE}}{R_E + \dfrac{R_{TH}}{\beta + 1}}
With V_{BE} = 0.70\,\text{V} and \beta \approx 150:

I_{C(\text{calc})} = \frac{1.70 - 0.70}{100 + \dfrac{12880}{151}} = \frac{1.00}{100 + 85.3} = \frac{1.00}{185.3} = 5.40\,\text{mA}
Experimental: I_{C(\text{meas})} = 5.25\,\text{mA}, deviation of only 2.8\%.

Circuit 3 (R_E shorted): The stabilizing term I_E R_E vanishes. Base current:

I_B = \frac{V_{TH} - V_{BE}}{R_{TH}} = \frac{1.70 - 0.72}{12880} = 76.1\,\mu\text{A}
This drives I_C = 9.55\,\text{mA}, dropping V_C to 2.45\,\text{V}. Any temperature increase causes V_{BE} to decrease by -2.2\,\text{mV}/^\circ\text{C} and \beta to increase, triggering thermal runaway without R_E.
content.conclusion: Experiment 301 verified the fundamental principles governing BJTs in common-emitter configuration. The input characteristic confirmed exponential p-n diode behavior with knee potential 0.65\,\text{V}. The output family mapped Cutoff, Active Linear, and Saturation zones. The DC load line established V_{CE(\text{cutoff})} = 12.0\,\text{V} and I_{C(\text{sat})} = 10.91\,\text{mA}. The self-biased divider provides a stable Q-point (V_{CE} = 5.75\,\text{V},\; I_C = 5.25\,\text{mA}), and R_E provides essential negative feedback preventing thermal instability.

questions.question: Compare theoretical predictions with laboratory measurements.

learnings: Measurement Competence: Distinguishing absolute node potentials (V_B, V_C, V_E) from differential junction voltages (V_{BE}, V_{CE}).
Semiconductor Operating States: Diagnosing BJT state from V_{BE} and V_{CE} alone.
Load Line Visualization: How V_{CC}, R_C, R_E define the operational envelope.
Thermal Stability Engineering: How emitter degeneration prevents Q-point drift.
